title: How to prepare for a Vedic astrology consultation
excerpt: What details to gather, how to frame your questions, and what a responsible consultation can and cannot tell you.
cover_alt: A hand-drawn north-Indian style birth chart on cream paper
body:
Gather accurate birth details

A Vedic chart is calculated from your date, time and place of birth. The time matters most: the ascendant (lagna) changes roughly every two hours, and house placements shift with it. If you have a birth certificate or hospital record, use the time recorded there. If you only have an approximate time, say so when you book.

Decide what you want to ask

A focused consultation is a more useful one. Before the session, write down two or three questions that matter most to you right now, such as a career decision, a family matter or the timing of a move. Questions phrased as "What should I consider when…" tend to lead to richer conversations than "Will X happen?"

Understand what a chart offers

Jyotish is a traditional interpretive system. A chart reading can offer a framework for reflection, a way of thinking about timing, and a structured conversation with someone experienced in the tradition. It cannot guarantee outcomes, and it does not replace medical, legal or financial advice.

Bring a notebook

You will hear terms such as dasha (planetary period), transit and nakshatra. Noting them down, along with any suggestions discussed, makes it easier to reflect afterwards.

After the session

Give yourself time to think before acting on anything. Any suggested practices are optional. The decisions remain yours.

title: Non-invasive Vastu for rented homes
excerpt: You can't move walls in a rented flat. Here is how Vastu principles are applied through arrangement, usage and light instead.
cover_alt: A sunlit apartment living room with plants near an east-facing window
body:
Start with orientation

Every Vastu review begins with directions. Stand at the centre of your home with a compass app and mark north on a simple floor plan. This one sheet of paper is the most useful thing you can bring to a consultation.

Work with usage, not walls

In a rented home, the structure is fixed, but how each room is used is not. Which room you sleep in, where you work, and where you keep stored items are all choices that Vastu guidance can address.

Placement and arrangement

The direction you face while working, the position of your bed and the placement of heavy furniture are common subjects of non-invasive suggestions. These are reversible and cost little or nothing.

Light and clutter

Traditional Vastu texts give weight to natural light and open movement through a space. Clearing entrances and keeping light-filled areas uncluttered are among the simplest steps.

Know the limits

Some features of a layout cannot be changed without construction, and an honest consultation will say so. Vastu is a traditional discipline; it complements, but never replaces, safety or structural advice.

title: Sunday mornings, Surya Hora and a better study routine
excerpt: Why Jyotish links Sunday mornings with the Sun, what Surya Hora is, and how to turn the idea into a simple, practical study habit.
cover_alt: Flyer about studying during Surya Hora on Sunday mornings
body:
If your child sleeps in late every Sunday, they may be missing what Jyotish traditionally treats as one of the most powerful study times of the week.

Sunday and the Sun

In Jyotish and numerology, Sunday is associated with Surya, the Sun. Surya is traditionally linked with leadership, concentration, confidence and intelligence.

What is Surya Hora?

A hora is a planetary hour. The traditional system assigns each hour of the day to a planet, and on Sunday the first hora after sunrise belongs to the Sun. It is believed that studying during Surya Hora supports focus, clarity and self-confidence.

Right time, not only more time

What I tell my students and parents is simple: it isn't only about studying more, it's also about studying at the right time. Whatever your view of planetary hours, an early, quiet, well-rested start is a habit that helps almost every learner.

Making it work at home

  • Agree a fixed Sunday wake-up time the night before, and keep screens out of the bedroom.
  • Use the first hour after sunrise for the subject that needs the most concentration.
  • Keep the study space tidy and free of distractions.
  • Pair the routine with a positive mindset and discipline through the week.

A routine like this won't replace steady work, but combined with a positive mindset and a distraction-free environment, it can help take academic performance to the next level.

title: More tuition is not always the answer
excerpt: Three tuitions, two coaching classes, one very tired child, and marks that won't move. When the block isn't the syllabus, here is where to look.
cover_alt: Illustration of a worried student with shaking hands in an exam hall
body:
Three tuitions. Two coaching classes. One very tired child. And still, the marks don't move.

When the problem isn't the syllabus

Coaching fills the notebook. It cannot always calm the mind. When a child's hand shakes in the exam hall, or they blank on a chapter they knew the night before, that is rarely a syllabus problem, and another class won't fix it.

What handwriting can show

In graphology, handwriting is read as a trace of how a person is thinking and feeling as they write. Changes in pressure, spacing, size or speed can point to where a child is getting stuck: rushing, holding back, losing focus partway through. It isn't a diagnosis, but it is a useful place to start a conversation.

A five-minute check you can do today

Open your child's notebook and compare a page written at the start of a study session with one written at the end. Look at whether the writing stays the same size, whether lines drift, and whether the pressure changes. Then ask your child how they were feeling at each point.

If you would like the free five-minute notebook checklist, message CHECKLIST on WhatsApp and it will be sent to you.

When to look further

If your child's distress is persistent, or you suspect a learning difficulty, speak with their school and a qualified professional. Handwriting work is a complement to that support, not a replacement.
